newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Lebanon won't attend Mideast economic summit - PM.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon won't attend Mideast economic summit - PM.

text.p: Lebanon's Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri said on Thursday his country would not attend the Middle East economic summit scheduled for November in Qatar because Israel did not respect the peace process agreements.

Hariri, who earlier discussed the summit with King Hassan, told a news conference: "Lebanon will not attend the expected Qatar meeting in November...We have already taken the decision which reflects our situation as Lebanese."
Israel occupies a strip of Lebanon's territory in the south of the country.
The summit, launched in Casablanca in 1994, was expected to promote peace in the Middle East through trade and economic cooperation between Israel and its Arab neighbours.

Saudi Arabia has said it will not attend. Other important Arab states, including Egypt and Morocco, have decided to wait and see whether anything happens in peace talks between Israel and the Palestinians.
Hariri said he discussed several international issues with King Hassan including the deadlocked Middle East peace process.
"The peace process faces a serious crisis due to the Israeli position which does not respect the previous peace agreements with Arab countries," he said.
Asked about the possibility of replacing Israeli troops by a U.N. multinational force in southern Lebanon, Hariri said:

"These are political manoeuvres to improve the Israeli government image...It should be noted that up to now Israel did not recognise the U.N. Security Council Resolution 425 which stipulates Israel should withdraw from Lebanese territories."
Hariri urged Arab states to set up "a free trade zone for agriculture goods" and promote wider trade exchanges.
"Arab countries, which have a surplus of agricultural products, import from abroad foodstuffs estimated at $30 billion every year...This is not normal," he said.
"We should set up a free trade zone for agricultural goods and boost trade exchanges between the Arab countries," he said.
Hariri, winding up his three-day visit to Morocco, said he examined the issue with King Hassan and would discuss it with other Arab leaders.
